name: Jade Farah

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We don't work for AI companies, employers, unions or any party, and we're not selling anything. Everything you say stays confidential, so feel free to tell me what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. To start, can you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm a troubleshooter for a rural electric co-op, which means when your lights go out at two in the morning, I'm the one who drives out. I work mostly alone in a bucket truck, number 31, covering about four hundred miles of line through farmland and forest. A normal day is a few planned jobs, a fuse here, a meter there, and then whatever the radio throws at me. I like being trusted to sort it out myself, and I don't like ice storms or people who think I can fix the whole county in an hour.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Who's at home when you get back?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: My husband Sami is a mechanic at the county garage, and we've got a son who's fourteen and a daughter who's ten. We've got a mortgage on a house just off Route 9, and a good chunk saved, because both of us grew up with parents who were always short. I don't use those AI things. I've got a flip-style work phone and a paper map book in the truck, and I'm faster with that than the young guys are with their screens.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say, well, there you go, all that fuss for nothing. Probably wouldn't say much more, I'm not one for posting. At the co-op office somebody would make a joke and that would be it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It doesn't mean anything for me, because it never did. Out on Route 9 at night, there's no computer coming to splice a broken line in the rain. I'd be quietly glad I didn't waste my time learning it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Same as always. Keep working my on-call weeks, keep the savings growing, pay the mortgage, take the kids camping in August. I don't see anything to change.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. Pretty much like any other Tuesday.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd be glad you didn't learn it. Did anyone push you to?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The co-op sent everyone an email about an AI outage tool last year. I deleted it. My manager asked if I'd tried it, and I said I've got thirty-one years of Route 9 in my head, so no. Well, nineteen years, but it felt like thirty-one.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there anything about your work that already feels like it's changing?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The smart meters, a bit. They tell the office a house is out before the farmer even calls. That's fine, that's useful. It still takes me to drive out and fix it.

S0.say: Well, there you go, all that fuss for nothing. I wouldn't say much more than that, because I'm not one for posting.
S0.think: It doesn't mean anything for me because it never did; there's no computer coming to splice a broken line on Route 9 at night. I'd be quietly glad I didn't waste time learning it.
S0.do: Carries on with her on-call weeks, saving and mortgage payments as usual. Takes the family camping in August as planned.
S0.quote: My manager asked if I'd tried it, and I said I've got thirty-one years of Route 9 in my head, so no.
S0.fieldNote: Jade is self-reliant and unbothered, with a dry humour and a strong sense of her own competence. She resists AI on principle but accepts technology like smart meters that clearly helps. She doesn't blame anyone; to her the hype was simply noise.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many tasks in many jobs. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. But most people still have work, and society has time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say let's see what actually works and what doesn't. Some of it will help and some of it will be junk, same as everything. I wouldn't be making speeches about it either way.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, I think it hits the office more than me. The co-op might cut a dispatcher or two and I'd miss them. But someone still has to go out in the truck, and in the country, that's going to be a person for a good while.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep doing my job and learn only what the co-op made me learn. If they put a tablet in the truck, fine, I'd use it, grudgingly. We'd keep saving like we do, maybe a bit more, just in case.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Mostly calm. A little tired just thinking about new tablets.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who in the office would you miss?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Lorraine on the radio. She can tell from my voice if I'm cold or tired and she'll send someone out to back me up without me asking. No tablet in the world is going to hear that I'm shivering and send Hank with a thermos.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said 'just in case.' In case of what?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In case the co-op decides it can run with fewer of us. I don't think it would, but I've seen budgets do strange things. Having a cushion means I don't have to worry about it at night.

S1.say: Let's see what actually works and what doesn't, because some of it will help and some will be junk. I wouldn't make speeches about it either way.
S1.think: It hits the office more than me, and I'd miss a dispatcher or two if they went. Out in the country, someone still has to go out in the truck, and that'll be a person for a good while.
S1.do: Keeps doing her job and learns only what the co-op requires, using a truck tablet if issued. Saves a bit more as a precaution.
S1.feel: Mostly calm, a little weary at the thought of new tablets.
S1.quote: No tablet in the world is going to hear that I'm shivering and send Hank with a thermos.
S1.fieldNote: Jade's calm comes from rural distance and a strong cushion rather than from enthusiasm. Her real attachment is to people like Lorraine who look after her, and that is what she fears losing. She's pragmatic and doesn't point fingers.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. With robots it reaches hands-on work too. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say I'll believe it when I see a robot drive Route 9 in an ice storm. I'd keep it short, and I wouldn't be joining any protests. People would probably think I was in denial.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, it'd shake me more than I'd show. I'm not going to learn a whole new trade, and I don't want to. If robots really can climb and drive, then the co-op would eventually need fewer of us, but I think the country would be last, and I'd probably hang on for a while.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd stop any big spending, like the new truck Sami wants, and keep our cash safe. I'd keep working as long as they'd have me and wait to see how real it was before doing anything drastic. If it came to it, I'd look at what the county or other co-ops are hiring, since there are plenty nearby.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious. A tight feeling in my chest I'd ignore until I couldn't.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said people would think you were in denial. Would they be right?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Maybe a bit. Denial's got me through a lot of ice storms; you don't think about the drop, you think about the next bolt. I'd rather focus on the next job than the end of the world.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to Sami about the truck?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say not this year. He'd grumble, he's been looking at that pickup for two years. But he grew up the same as me, he'd understand once I showed him the numbers.

S2.say: I'll believe it when I see a robot drive Route 9 in an ice storm. I'd keep it short and stay away from protests, even if people thought I was in denial.
S2.think: It would shake me more than I'd show, because I won't learn a whole new trade. If robots can climb and drive the co-op needs fewer of us, but the country would go last and I'd probably hang on a while.
S2.do: Holds off on big purchases, including her husband's new truck, and keeps cash safe. Keeps working and waits to see how real the change is, then checks what the county and other co-ops are hiring if needed.
S2.feel: Anxious, a tight chest she'd ignore for as long as she could.
S2.quote: Denial's got me through a lot of ice storms; you don't think about the drop, you think about the next bolt.
S2.fieldNote: Jade admits to using denial as a coping skill and frames it in climbing terms. Her strong savings and rural setting keep her from alarm, but her refusal to retrain leaves her with few moves beyond waiting. Her husband's truck is the concrete casualty.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is a long time and plenty can change. I'd tell people not to panic and to keep their savings up. Not much more than that.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Truthfully, five years would help. I'd be forty-eight, the kids would be nearly grown, and we'd have paid a lot more off the house. I'm still not keen on learning new tricks, but I'd have time to think about what I'd do if the co-op cut back.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Put extra into the mortgage every month so it's smaller when it hits. Keep working, and maybe, if the co-op offered training on running the robots, I'd go along to see, but I wouldn't sign up for anything on my own. Mainly I'd watch and wait.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy. It's there, but it's not keeping me up yet.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would make you sign up for training on your own?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If I saw robot trucks working other co-ops' lines and doing it well. Then I'd know it's real and I'd have to. I don't like learning things that might not last.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would your daughter think if robots were fixing the lines?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: She'd think it was cool, she loves robots. She'd probably name the thing and want to ride in it, and I'd be standing there with my hooks wondering what I'm for.

S3.say: Five years is a long time and plenty can change, so don't panic and keep your savings up. I wouldn't say much more than that.
S3.think: Five years would help, since I'd be forty-eight, the kids nearly grown and more of the house paid off. I'm not keen on new tricks, but I'd have time to think about what to do if the co-op cut back.
S3.do: Pays extra on the mortgage every month to shrink it before the change. Keeps working and goes to co-op robot training only if offered, otherwise watches and waits.
S3.feel: Uneasy, present but not keeping her up yet.
S3.quote: She'd probably name the thing and want to ride in it, and I'd be standing there with my hooks wondering what I'm for.
S3.fieldNote: More time lets Jade fall back on what she trusts: paying down debt and waiting. She'd only retrain once she's seen proof elsewhere. Her daughter's delight in robots, contrasted with her own sense of losing purpose, was a striking moment.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is a long way off, and I'll deal with it when it gets closer. Plenty of predictions have come and gone. I'd tell the young guys to keep their skills sharp and their savings up.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, ten years is fine for me, mostly. I'd be fifty-three, the mortgage close to gone, the kids out of school. If the robots came in then, I'd probably be one of the last troubleshooters in the county, and I could live with that.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Nothing much the first year. Keep working, keep saving, keep paying down the house. If the co-op starts trialling robots in year five or six, I'd pay attention then, maybe think about early retirement around fifty-five.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, in the background. Like a dentist appointment you booked a long time ago.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd be one of the last. How would that feel?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Lonely, probably. But I like working alone anyway. Being the last one out on Route 9 isn't the worst thing; somebody's got to turn the lights off.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Your son would be twenty-four in 2036. Would you want him in the trade?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: He's talking about it already, he likes coming out to the yard. I'd tell him to learn it but also learn something else alongside, maybe the mechanics side like his dad. I don't know what else to tell him, honestly.

S4.say: Ten years is a long way off, and I'll deal with it when it gets closer, because plenty of predictions have come and gone. I'd tell the young ones to keep their skills sharp and savings up.
S4.think: Ten years is mostly fine for me, because at fifty-three the mortgage would be nearly gone and the kids out of school. I'd probably be one of the last troubleshooters in the county and I could live with that.
S4.do: Changes little in the first year and keeps working, saving and paying down the house. Watches for co-op robot trials around year five or six and considers early retirement around fifty-five.
S4.feel: Uneasy in the background, like a dentist appointment booked long ago.
S4.quote: Being the last one out on Route 9 isn't the worst thing; somebody's got to turn the lights off.
S4.fieldNote: Ten years lets Jade fall back almost fully on her plan to keep going and retire a bit early. She would even accept being the last troubleshooter in the county. Her advice to her son, learn a second skill, is the one forward-looking step she takes.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The fast one, AGI by 2028, because I wouldn't have time to pay the house down or think. What would help is the co-op being straight with us about what's coming and keeping its people on, even if it's doing different work. Sami and I are fine for a while, but I'd like to know there's a plan.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Maybe ask about the country. Everybody talks about cities and offices. Out here a downed line means a dairy farm with no milking machine, and somebody's got to get there before the cows get loud.

headlineQuote: Out here a downed line means a dairy farm with no milking machine, and somebody's got to get there before the cows get loud.
portrait: Jade Farah is a 43-year-old troubleshooter for a rural electric co-op who works alone in a bucket truck along Route 9, married to a mechanic, with two children and solid savings. She's dry, self-reliant and proud of her paper map book, and she never uses AI tools. She stays calm in the hype and gradual scenarios, becomes anxious but holds back on spending and waits when AGI comes in two years, and settles back to unease with more warning. Her plan is to pay down the house, keep working and possibly retire early. She doesn't blame anyone in particular and copes by focusing on the next job.
biggestWorry: AGI by 2028 worries her most, because there wouldn't be time to pay down the house or think.
whatWouldHelp: The co-op being honest about what's coming and keeping its people on, even doing different work, so she knows there's a plan.
